text.text:
Yann LeCun just launched AMI, and named it "friend" (ami in French 🇫🇷). 

LeCun left Meta in November, raised $1.03B in the largest seed round ever by a European startup, at a $3.5B valuation announced March 10, 2026. The company is called Advanced Machine Intelligence. 

His core argument: "The real revolution is not AI replacing humans, but AI helping humans think better, plan better, and understand the real world." And: LLMs "don't really deal with the real world", they can pass the bar exam but can't navigate physical reality, which is why we don't have domestic robots or level-5 self-driving cars.

In a world of agents and automation, the most human thing you can build is something that helps people think better.

text.text:
I was in tears after reading a message on Slack. I think it was… tears of pride.

My designer colleague texted me her plan for guiding agentic coders. She would write skills. Not just markdown! She’d include executable scripts to do heavy lifting.

In my mind I went “SHE FIGURED IT OUT! She learned to ride the bike!”

Just a few days ago, I gave her access to AI coding agents and gave a short tutorial to agents, skills and context engineering. “It’s more art than science. It’s all about intuition.”

I wouldn’t use the word mentor or mentorship.

I wouldn’t say I upskilled her. It’s too imposing.

“My ideas aren’t too bonkers after all” - was how I was feeling back then.

The act was not selfless tho. It’s probably a form of leaving my mark on the world. In capable people.

So proud of the people I work with everyday.

text.text:
Yesterday marks the end of my one-year internship at Pints AI, and it feels strangely bittersweet.

When I first stepped in, I thought this year would mostly be about learning new technologies and gaining industry experience. It was, but it was also so much more than that. It challenged the way I think, pushed me to question existing paradigms, and taught me that growth often comes from moments when you’re unsure but willing to try anyway.

There were days where things worked beautifully, and days where nothing seemed to go according to the gameplan. But those moments ended up being the most valuable. They taught me how to adapt, how to think deeper about problems, and how to keep moving forward even when the path wasn’t obvious.

What made this journey truly special, though, were the people. To my mentors, Gabriel L. and Soksedtha Ly, thank you for your patience, guidance, and for trusting me with real problems that helped me grow beyond what I expected. And to all the amazing coworkers I had the chance to work alongside: thank you for the conversations, the collaboration, and the little moments that made the workplace feel welcoming every day.

I’m leaving this chapter not just with new skills, but with new perspectives, stronger curiosity, and a deeper appreciation for the people who make meaningful work possible. Grateful for everything this year has taught me. 

On to the next chapter.

text.text:
𝗧𝘄𝗼 𝗬𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗮 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗽 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗱 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗜 𝗦𝗲𝗲 𝗠𝘆 𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝗟𝗶𝗳𝗲

Two years in a startup did not just change my career. It reshaped how I understand my purpose and how I choose to live the one life I have been given.

Growing up, I was always the kid who stayed behind the scenes. I never felt good enough. I assumed I would stay there forever, terrified that if I ever stepped into the light, the world would finally see what I already believed about myself.

I remember walking into work one morning feeling a heavy sense of dread. I asked myself, "Why am I working a job with low pay, long hours, and 100% uncertainty about whether any of this will even work?" Then I looked around and saw my teammates. These were young people who were not chasing paychecks. They were chasing impact. For them, "Product-Market Fit" was not some sterile concept from a textbook. It was the only way forward if they wanted to solve a real human problem. Something clicked in me that day.

We were building in Education Technology. And having worked in this space, I honestly believe most edtech products are fluff. They fail to see what learning actually is. Learning is not about telling someone, "This is wrong, and here are the concepts you need to get it right." Most products never bother asking why a student has a mental block, or why they struggle to connect the dots and put them into words.

That experience taught me something I carry into every project now. Building with AI should never start with automating existing workflows. It should start with a bigger question. If you have access to technology that can synthesise data at scale, what problems can you now solve that were never possible to solve before?

This is how I see my life now. I refuse to be a developer who replicates manual, repetitive tasks into automated scripts. I want to look at a broken process and find the real bottleneck. I want to find the most significant change I can make with AI to bring the highest value to someone in the shortest amount of time.
This shift in perspective has completely changed how I feel about work. The pressure of the rat race is gone. Life is no longer about just getting the job done, making money, and surviving. Solving real problems and bringing positive change to people is actually exciting. And I have come to believe that if I am good enough to provide genuine value, others will see that value in me too.

Life is too short to reduce it to a climb up the corporate ladder. I would rather spend it building things that matter.
